caseno: Appeal from Original Order No. 227 of 1987
lawyer:
Appeal dismissed. Fazlul Karim, Advocate, with A.K.M. Nurunnabi Khan, Advocate. ----- For the Appellant. 
A.T.M. Monwaruddin, Advocate, with Shirin Nahar, Advocate. ------ For the Respondent No.1 
B. Hossain, Advocate. ------ For the Respondent No.2
parties:
Harun-or-Rashid Talukder ------ Appellant 
Vs. 
District Manager, Pubali Bank, Jamalpur ------ Respondent
full_judgment:
Mustafa Kamal, J:-This First Miscellaneous Appeal has been preferred under Article 36(1) of the Bangladesh Legal Practitioners and Bar Council Order, 1972 (P.O. No. 46 of 1972) against the judgment and order dated 5.7.87 passed by Tribunal No. II of the Bangladesh Bar Council in Tribunal Case No. 4 of 1983, finding the appellant guilty of gross professional misconduct under Clause (1) of Article 32 of P.O. No.46 of 1972 and suspending him for a period of 8 years and debarring him from practicing in any Court or authority in Bangladesh during the period of suspension with immediate effect. 

 2. The proceeding before the Tribunal was initiated by P.W. 1 Md. Liakat Ali Khan, District Manager, Pubali Bank, Jamalpur Branch by addressing a letter of complaint on 6.6.83 to the President Bangladesh Bar Council, invoking legal action against the appellant on the facts stated therein. The appellant replied to the allegations by his letter dated 25.8.83 to the President, Bangladesh Bar Council. Thereafter the Bangladesh Bar Council proceeded against the appellant by instituting Case No.4 of 1983 before the Tribunal No. II. Issues were framed on 11.2.84. The appellant was also permitted to amend certain portions of his reply dated 25.8.83. 

 4. The said Tribunal discussing the entire case and evidence on record by its judgment and order under appeal found the appellant guilty of gross professional misconduct and sentenced him as aforesaid. 

 7. It is further admitted by both the parties that the said Money Suit No. 3A/79 was decreed exparte in favour of the Pubali Bank. Upon the instruction of the bank the appellant filed Money Execution Case No.2 of 1980 of the 4th Court of Subordinate Judge, Mymensingh. Jamalpur was made a district and in December, 1980 the District judge's Court at Jamalpur started functioning. The appellant shifted his place of practice from Mymensingh to Jamalpur shortly thereafter. The records of the said execution case were sent to Jamalpur and the Money Execution Case was re-numbered as Money Execution Case No. 4 of the Court of Subordinate Judge, Jamalpur. 

 8. Thereafter the story of the complainant and the appellant differs. The complainant contends that during the pendency of Money Execution Case No.4 of 1982 in which the petitioner bank prayed for realisation of the decrial amount by sale of the attached property, namely, plot No. 1489 of mouza Chandra comprising an area of 1.04 acre and plot No. 1082 of mouza Shinghajani measuring 10 acre, the appellant being the engaged lawyer of the bank and knowing full well that the above-mentioned properly was the subject matter of the aforesaid execution case, purchased the said land in his own name and in the name of his wife and children and also in the benami of his cousin D.W. 2 Md. Mahfuzul Hoq Talukdcr by 4 registered kabalas dated 25.8.81, Ext.3, 3(1), 3(2) and 3(3). When the bank came to know of this transaction the complainant P.W. 1 requested the appellant to return the brief. He returned the case file P.W. 1 also requested the appellant to pay up the bank's dues assuring that in such an event the bank will not take any legal action against the appellant. But the appellant did not comply with that request. Thereafter a legal notice was served on the appellant demanding the bank's money within a certain period failing which the matter would be referred to the Bar Council [or professional misconduct. The appellant received the notice, but did not reply. The bank has been affected by the purchase in question. The complainant prayed that suitable action be taken against the appellant for gross professional misconduct. It was further stated by the complainant in his evidence that the schedule-property of the execution case is under the occupation of the appellant. He has started construction thereon and has since started his professional activities therefrom by opening his chamber thereon. He is also residing there with his family. 

 9. It is admitted by the appellant that by 5 different registered deeds dated 25.8.81 the appellant has purchased part of the suit property under attachment in his name and in the names of his wife and children. D.W.2 Md. Mahfuzul Hoq Talukder, his cousin, is the co-purchaser of the-remaining part of the suit property. Since purchase he and D.W. 2 have possessed the suit property under attachment. 7 1/ 2 acres of land covered by the said sale deeds are situated at Jamalpur town and the appellant has himself stated that he has already constructed puce buildings thereon. His explanation is that P.W. 2 Sk. Nowsher Ali who was manager of Pubali Bank, Main Branch, Jamalpur from 30.12.74 to 13.8.81 made an unauthorised advance of Tk. 50,000/- to the defendant Kafiluddin Islami in 1975. He obtained an equitable mortgage of the suit property under attachment from Kafiluddin Islami, as security for the loan, but there was no registration of the mortgage. When Jamalpur was made a separate district and the District Judge's Court started functioning at Jamalpur, the appellant shifted his practice from Mymensingh to Jamalpur. P.W.2 Sk. Nowsher Ali gave out in June 1981 that he was going to be transferred from Jamalpur. P.W. 2 pressed the appellant hard for an early disposal of the aforesaid money execution case. At about this time defendant Kafiluddin was also trying to sell out the suit property under attachment to third parties. Successive signboards affixed upon the suit property stating that the same was under attachment were mysteriously disappearing for which P.W.2 sought police help. P.W.2 came to an understanding with defendant Kafiluddin that the suit properly would be sold for realisation of bank's dues. P.W.2 requested the appellant to purchase the suit property, but he declined stating that a lawyer was under a legal disability to purchase the same. Besides, the appellant had no fund to buy the property. The appellant was given the proposal that he was required to pay Tk. 75,000/-, the bank's dues, to the bank by installment. He needed to pay defendant Kafiluddin the balance of the consideration money. At this stage the appellant agreed to purchase the suit property for Tk. 10,05,00/- out of which the bank's claim was Tk.80,000/- only and the appellant actually paid Tk. 30,000/- only to defendant Kafiluddin. The appellant did not pay any money to the bank at the time of purchase. Uptil now he has not paid even a single penny to the bank. It is also the case of the appellant that on the basis of mutual agreement between the parties. Tk. 5000/- was remitted by the bank in favour of defendant Kafiluddin at the instance of P.W. 2 Nowsher Ali. As the appellant had no sufficient funds to buy the suit property, he requested his cousin D.W. 2 Mahfuzul Hoq Talukder to join him to purchasing the suit property. P.W. 2 Nowsher Ali came to the chamber of the appellant many times in connection with the above claim of the bank. Mr. Nowsher Ali was transferred and he made over charge to his successor P.W. 1 Liakat Ali on 13.8.81. The new manager was also in the know of the matter. The appellant was informed by a letter dated 18.9.81 that he was no longer the legal advisor of the bank and that Mr. Amjad Hossain, another Advocate, replaced him. After making representations to the Managing Director of the bank and having received no reply thereto the appellant made over charge to the said Mr. Amjad Hossain. The appellant came to know of the demand of the bank by legal notice dated 2.11.82. According to the appellant himself he has filed as many as 3 applications under Order 21 Rule 58 C.P.C. for being added as a party to the aforesaid execution case, 2 which were rejected and the last one of which is still pending. He has also stated in his reply to the allegations of the complainant that he filed O.C. Suit No. 71/83 on 26.6.83 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Jamalpur, for a declaration that the Pubali Bank had no claim on him with respect to the land of the aforesaid money execution case. 

 10. Mr. Fazlul Karim, learned Advocate for the appellant has based his submissions solely and completely on the aforesaid story of the appellant and has soulful argue, in the first place, that the appellant having not acquired "an interest" adverse to the bank in the property involved in the execution case, is not guilty of professional misconduct. He has argued secondly that it is under circumstances of a peculiar nature that the appellant had merely exercised an ill judgment. He became the victim of an inducement and was merely used as a pawn by the outgoing manager P.W. 2 SK. Nowsher Ali. The Tribunal did not notice the effect of the inducement made by P.W. 2 Nowsher Ali. Lastly, Mr. Fazlul Karim submits, the facts and circumstances of the case do not warrant imposition of a harsh sentence of suspension from practice for 8 years. At best, the appellant can be reprimanded. 

 "(I) An Advocate shall not acquire an interest adverse to a client in the property or interest involved in the case." 

 12. Mr. Fazlul Karim submits that an Advocate cannot acquire an interest adverse to his client in the property until and unless by the transaction in question he acquires a title to the property. Both Section 64 and Order 21 Rule 64 C.P.C. make It quite clear that if a person purchases a property under attachment without permission from the Court then the whole transaction is void. The attached properly is liable to sale notwithstanding the unauthorised purchase. Therefore, the bank has sustained no loss and has incurred no disability at all by the appellant's purchase of the suit property. It's remedy of sale of the suit property under attachment IS still available, notwithstanding the appellant's purchase. Mr. Fazlul Karim argues that when the appellant has thus acquired no title to the suit property under attachment by viture of Section 64 c.P.c. then it cannot be said that he has acquired any interest adverse to the bank in the property. He is, therefore, not guilty of any professional misconduct. Specially Clause (I) of Chapter II is inapplicable to him. 

 13. It is difficult to uphold the aforesaid contention of Mr. Fazlul Karim. A client does not always have a proprietary interest in the suit property. He may have a possessory interest, a contingent interest and even a trespasser's interest in the suit property. It is enough to attract the mischief of Clause(l) of Chapter II if the Advocate engaged by the client transgresses upon any such interest held by the client. In the present case the bank's interest in the suit property under attachment is total. It has an interest in the right, title and possession of the suit property. Upon his own admission the appellant sought to create a title in him by purchasing the suit property admittedly under attachment at a time when he was the engaged Advocate of the bank to conduct the execution case. He admits that he has not only taken possession of the suit property under attachment but has also constructed a building thereon. To acquire an interest adverse to the bank in the instant case it is not necessary that the appellant should acquire a valid title to the suit property. It is enough that he has created several documents of title in his favour and has entered into possession of the suit property. He has thereby prejudiced the interest of the bank in the suit property. On his own admission he has filed as many as 3 applications, one of which is pending, for being added as a third party to the execution case. He has thus sought to place himself in the shoes of defendant Kafiluddin. The bank is thus obliged to prosecute the execution case not only against defendant Kafiluddin but also against the bank's own lawyer, the appellant, who is claiming an interest in the suit property, valid or otherwise. It is because of the appellant's repeated efforts to get himself added as a third party in the execution proceedings that the execution proceedings have been delayed. The appellant has thus compromised his position as a conducting lawyer of the case. Not only that, he has himself stated in his reply to the complainant's allegation (at page 42 of the paper book) that on 26.6.83 he has filed O.C. Suit No. 71/83 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Jamalpur, praying that the bank has no claim upon him with respect to the land of Money Execution Case No. 4/82 pending in that Court. Apart from proceeding against defendant Kafiluddin the bank is now saddled with the additional burden of facing and meeting the appellant's pleas and submissions. It is absolutely immaterial whether by virtue of Ext. 3 series the appellant has acquired a valid title to the suit property under attachment or not. This issue will be decided in an appropriate forum by the concerned parties. For the purpose of disposing of this professional misconduct case the Tribunal will only see the various kinds of interest that a client has over the property or interest involved in the case and as to whether the Advocate concerned has acquired any of the interests adverse to the client. The facts arc palpably clear and we have no manner of doubt that the Tribunal has come to the correct conclusion that the appellant in purchasing the suit property under attachment and in taking possession thereof and constructing a building thereon has definitely acquired an interest adverse to the bank in the suit property. 

 14. Of course Mr. Fazlul Karim next submits that if the appellant has been able to show that everything was done in the interest of the bank as part of a package with the knowledge and with the blessing of the local manager, then his action may be branded as reprehensible, but he cannot be saddled with the delinquency of professional misconduct. He further submits that the appellant has exercised a mere ill judgment and that the circumstances were such that he was induced to exercise such an ill judgment without realising the consequence thereof. 

 15. The appellant contends that the loan given to defendant Kafiluddin was an unauthorised advance. There was no registered deed of mortgage of the suit property. P.W. 2 Sk. Nowsher Ali was nervous about this particular case because the advance money would be realised from him when he would leave the station if it still remained unpaid. So he was in a hurry to realise the loan and it was on his initiative that a tripartite agreement was made between him, the appellant and defendant Kafiluddin providing that the property would be purchased by the appellant for only Tk. 1,05,000/- out of which defendant Kafiluddin would be paid only Tk. 30,000/-. The appellant would pay to the bank Tk. 80,000/- by installments. 

 17. It is in the evidence of the appellant deposing as D.W. 1 that the proposal to purchase the suit property was made to the appellant alone, but the appellant declined on the ground that as a lawyer he was under a legal disability to purchase the same. D.W. 1 has further stated that he agreed to purchase the suit property while it was suggested to him that he need not pay the bank's money all at a time. He could, pay by installments. He further said he had no sufficient fund. So he requested his cousin D.W. 2 to join them in purchasing the suit property. D.W. 1 nowhere makes out a case that in August, 1981 D.W. 2 was taken to the house of the appellant by defendant Kafiluddin and P.W. 2 Sk. Nowsher Ali was present there. D.W. 1 nowhere stated that on that occasion D.W. 2 came to know about the mortgaged property. It is nowhere in his evidence that P.W. 2 Sk. Nowsher Ali proposed to D.W. 1 and D.W. 2 jointly that they should purchase the property under attachment. D.W. 1 obviously was telling one story and D.W. 2 another. No one corroborates the other. Each one is telling a different story. 

 21. We find no material whatsoever that the advance made to defendant Kafiluddin was an unauthorised advance. We find no reason why P.W. 2 Sk. Nowsher Ali should be nervous about the advance before his departure from Jamalpur. He had made an advance to Kafiluddin in 1975. Kafiluddin failed to repay the loan. He instituted the money suit in 1979. He obtained ancabaret decree therein. The suit property was already under attachment before judgment. He has instituted a money execution case. When he left Jamalpur the position was that the suit property could be sold in the execution case at any time on the prayer of the bank. P.W. 2 Sk. Nowsher Ali had a perfect explanation both in respect of the loan and in respect of the steps he had taken for realising the loan. He had no compulsion to enter into a dubious verbal arrangement with the appellant for sale of the suit property. When he was enjoying the protection of a full-proof money execution case in his favour, he will be a fool indeed to enter into a verbal arrangement with the appellant and leave Jamalpur with not a single penny as actual recovery from that questionable transaction. Besides, he left no documents for his successor to follow up. We find that this is a completely cock and bull story invented by the appellant to save his skin. There were absolutely no compelling circumstances whatsoever necessitating the transfer of the suit property in favour of the appellant and his family members. We are quite clear in our mind from the evidence on record that the appellant wanted to strike a bargain in his favour by presenting the bank with a fait accompli. As soon as P.W.2Ieft Jamalpur he purchased the suit property by registered deeds, thinking that the incoming manager P.W.l will not know much about the matter. 

 22. His next defence is that the incoming manager P.W. 1 Liakat Ali in his bid to induct his distant relation Mr. Amjad Hossain Advocate as the legal adviser of Pubali Bank concocted a false story against the appellant and ultimately Mr. Amjad Hossain succeeded the appellant as the legal advisor of Pubali Bank, Jamalpur Branch. This is an another flight of imagination on the part of the appellant. Pubali Bank, Jamalpur Branch, had only the present execution case on its file. Mr. Amjad Hossain was asked to conduct only this case in place of the appellant after the questionable transaction came to the knowledge of the bank. Mr. Amjad Hossain was not a: recipient of a huge favour from the bank. The sale deeds in question were executed and registered 15 days after P.W. 2 Sk. Nowshaer Ali handed over charge. There is absolutely no evidence that his successor P.W. 1 Liakat Ali was also in the know of this alleged arrangement and in any case there is absolutely no evidence that P.W. 1 was in any way connected with the execution and registration of the sale deeds Ext. 3 series. There is also no evidence that Kafiluddin was allowed a remission of interest to the extent of Tk. 5,000/- because of the so-called arrangement. The evidence is that he was offered the remission provided he paid the bank's dues all at a time. He did not pay. 

 25. We have in details set out the facts, circumstances and evidence recorded in the case. We have no manner of hesitation in concurring with the Tribunal that "the purchase of the property in question by the opposite party (appellant) in his own name and in the names of his wife, children and cousin against the interest of the bank, whose cause he was representing, possession of the property in question by the opposite party (appellant), construction of building in a portion of the suit property, repeated attempts by him to block the progress of the money execution case in question are the clearest manifestations of the unholy desire of the opposite party (appellant) to acquire the attached property in question by any means, fair or foul, and in doing so he has clearly acted against the interest of his client, acting against his professional pledge and responsibility. Such course of action, indeed, deserves highest condemnation and calls for deterrent punishment". 

 "(1) An Advocate on the roll may, in the manner hereinafter provided be reprimanded, suspended or removed from practice if he is found guilty of professional or other misconduct." 

 27. Hence reprimand is the mildest punishment that can be meted out to an Advocate found guilty of professional or other misconduct. Suspension from practice is a sentence of a higher degree but it really belongs to the intermediate class of punishment. Removal from practice is the ultimate punishment that can be meted out to a delinquent Advocate. Considering that the appellant was of fairly advanced age and was in bruised health the Tribunal decided to award him the intermediate punishment of suspension from practice for 8 years. In the facts and circumstances of the case we do not think that the Tribunal misjudged the punishment that is appropriate in the case. The Tribunal acted completely within its discretion in not awarding the severest sentence in view of some extenuating circumstances. We do not find any reason why the intermediate punishment should now be relegated to the softest one. All the defense’s of the appellant have been proved to be completely cooked up. From the moment he received the legal notice from the bank up to the present moment his attitude is one of defiance, contest and challenge. He has no regrets, no remorse, no repentance either. He has chalked out a path of destructive self-justification. He must pay for his defiance. We find no extenuating circumstances whatsoever to reduce the sentence.
